# **Software Architecture Document** 

1. # **Introduction** {#introduction}

The paper describes the full architectural design of Second-Hand Vehicle Marketplace with Intelligent Search and Automated Inventory Processing System using various views within architecture. The paper captures the important architectural decisions that were made with respect to the system following the 4+1 Architecture Model (Use-Case View, Logical View, Process View, Deployment View, Implementation View, and a further Data View because of the amount of persistent data in the system)..

1. ## **Purpose** {#purpose}

The purpose of this document Software Architecture Document (SAD) is to make sure that the developers/testers know about the design/architecture and the reasoning behind it. This document will cover the architectural decisions that have been made, service boundaries, orchestration approach, data ownership, and deployment strategy so that the actual implementation is consistent with this architecture instead of doing it differently.

2. ## **Scope** {#scope}

It is a solution that enables users to upload their vehicles' inventories in bulk (CSV/JSON along with a zip file of pictures) with the input automatically processed via an asynchronous pipeline that stores and enhances the vehicle information with the buyers filtering and natural language-based searches. This paper details the architecture of all five microservices on the back-end (Auth & User, Marketplace, Ingestion & ETL, Admin, Notification), front-end application based on React, and AWS cloud infrastructure connecting them.

5. ## **Overview** {#overview}

The perspectives of architecture which this document refers to are discussed in section 2, alongside with their motivations. The objectives and constraints that were taken into account while developing the architecture are described in section 3\. The Use-Case View is discussed in section 4\. Section 5 is dedicated to the Logical View (decomposition on package and class level). The Process View (runtime behavior, concurrency) is described in section 6\. Section 7 is dedicated to the Deployment View (physical topology on AWS). The Implementation View (layering at source level between repositories) is covered in section 8\. Section 9 is dedicated to the Data View. Size/Performance and Quality Attributes are discussed in sections 10 and 11 respectively.

2. # **Architectural Representation**  {#architectural-representation}

* Six views are used in this paper to describe the stakeholder concerns:

* Use-Case View : The functional behavior observed by Guests, Buyers, Dealers, and Administrators; ties the other views to concrete examples.

* Logical View : Decomposition of the system into microservices packages, domain modules, and architecturally relevant classes.

* Process View : Behavior of the system at runtime; identifies concurrent execution components, sequences of executions, and process communications (HTTP, SQS, State Transitions of Step Functions, polling).

* Deployment View : The physical AWS platform the software operates on and the mapping of the logical components on that platform.

* Implementation View : Source code organization: repositories, layers within each service, and rules for layering.

* Data View : Persistent data model: the shared PostgreSQL schema and the object layout in S3.

Together these views implement the 4+1 architectural view model, extended with an explicit Data View given the system's substantial persistent-data and search-indexing requirements.

3. # **Architectural Goals and Constraints** {#architectural-goals-and-constraints}

   1. ## **Architectural Goals** {#architectural-goals}

* **Serverless first:** all backends are hosted on AWS Lambda as part of the AWS Free Tier plan and to manage idle server capacity in a system that is highly bursty and driven by uploads.

* Orchestrated ETL using a single worker Lambda: Ingestion and ETL pipelines have been implemented as AWS Step Functions state machines with a dedicated per-stage Lambda each, replacing the previous implementation where one single ETLWorker Lambda was being used. This brings in declarative retry mechanism, memory sizing per stage, and live execution graph, but with a trade-off of having more Lambdas to manage.

* Rules-first \+ LLM fallback normalization: Deterministic dictionary / regex based normalization takes care of the vast majority of fields from dealers for free; Groq (LLM) is only called when the rules are not able to determine the values.


* **Human-in-the-loop gate:** no value LIVE by Groq is released without a review by the dealer.Uploaded listings are placed in a PENDING\_REVIEW state and promoted to LIVE only via dealer's explicit action.Model-parity constraint (must hold): the embedding model and normalization dictionaries employed at ingestion and query time have to be exactly the same, from the same library, otherwise the two halves of the system are effectively using different vocabularies and vector spaces.

* **Two-tier dealer onboarding process:** rather than a single path for all dealers, the system distinguishes an Individual tier (just NIC, manual listing creation, a limited number of live listings) and a Business tier (certificate of business registration, unlimited bulk CSV/JSON/ZIP upload).Verification constraints and platform capabilities scale by tiers together so a casual individual seller will not be asked for paperwork that would make sense only for a small dealership and bulk uploads won't be enabled without corresponding business documentation.

* **Cross-service data isolation model:** within the shared RDS instance, each service exclusively owns its schema. Reads may cross service schemas via scoped, service-specific database roles (e.g. admin\_service\_role may SELECT from marketplace and ingestion tables for dashboarding); however, **writes are strictly isolated to each service's own schema**. Every service maintains absolute control over its own persistence data, ensuring strict microservice domain encapsulation. 

* **East-west service communication:** north-south requests from browser to services are passed through public API Gateway, while east-west calls between services (for example, Admin approving/deleting dealer), which are made using regular HTTP without Lambda, pass through internal API Gateway, thus providing identical code execution locally with Docker Compose and on the cloud platform AWS.

* **Shared reference data for fuzzy matching:** The pg\_trgm dictionaries (including those with alias promotion) exist in one tiny reference table called vehicle\_dictionaries, owned by marketplace-service. The ingestion-service queries it, caches a snapshot of it into memory upon container startup, using the same mechanism that is used by our ETL pipeline for Groq's make/model lookup, as opposed to embedding dictionaries into a shared library (not capable of supporting the indexed similarity() call) or an HTTP call per token.

* **One shared PostgreSQL instance, service-owned schemas:** The team made a conscious decision to use one Amazon RDS with per-service schema ownership instead of isolated per-service databases, considering the team's size and academic time frame; this ensures that issues such as migration history remain in one spot but the application code honors service boundaries.

* **Security by default**: JWT-based stateless authentication with revocable refresh tokens, role-based access control, and least-privilege IAM permissions scoped per Lambda function.

## **3.2 Constraints**  {#3.2-constraints}

* **Team and timeline constraints**: delivered by three undergraduate developers within a fixed academic schedule (26 June – 3 October), which favours a smaller number of well-justified architectural decisions over a maximally "correct" but harder-to-execute design.

* **Groq as the one non-AWS dependency**: every other component in the system lives inside AWS, but Groq is an external third-party API outside that boundary.Meaning it's the single point where the architecture must assume unavailability (rate limits, timeouts, outages) rather than treat failure as exceptional. 

* **Step Functions' 256 KB state payload limit**: a hard AWS platform ceiling, not a design choice. It's what forces the "pass S3 keys between states, never row data" pattern used throughout the pipeline.

* **Zero-cost/open-source tooling constraint**: every technology choice (NestJS, React, PostgreSQL, pgvector, Terraform, GitHub Actions) was made partly *because* it's free.

![][image1]

*Figure 1\. High-level architecture overview for AutoVault LK. The React SPA, public API Gateway, five NestJS microservices on Lambda, the Step Functions ETL pipeline, and shared AWS infrastructure (RDS, S3, SQS, SES). Solid arrows indicate synchronous calls or direct writes; dotted arrows indicate asynchronous or event-driven flows.*

## **3.3 Architecture Decision Records** {#3.3-architecture-decision-records}

### **3.3.1 ADR-001: Shared RDS Instance with Schema-Per-Service Isolation** {#3.3.1-adr-001:-shared-rds-instance-with-schema-per-service-isolation}

**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** July 2026  
**Deciders:** Group 25

**Context**  
The architecture is made up of five backend microservices, all of which have their own individual data domain. The team that is involved includes three undergraduates who are working in the academic time frame (June 26 – October 3\) and using AWS free tier budget. If we go for fully isolated databases for each service, costs will increase.

**Decision**

Use an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL instance (pgvector and pg\_trgm extensions) and logically isolate by creating five schemas for each of the services as auth, marketplace, ingestion, notifications, and admin. Each service will use a specific PostgreSQL user that has the least privilege on its schema only. Any cross-schema access must be allowed only via clearly defined grants.

**Consequences** 

● **Positive:** Single migration history; simpler local development; foreign keys (e.g., marketplace.vehicles.dealer\_id \-\> auth.users.id) remain enforceable at the database level; Free Tier budget is preserved.

● **Negative:** Services share a physical failure domain; schema migration coordination is required; true independent scaling of data stores is not possible.

● **Mitigation:** Service-owned schemas and role-based grants prevent accidental cross-service writes; centralized migrations are owned by a single database/ folder with explicit deployment ordering documented in the Implementation View.

**Alternatives Considered** 

| Alternative | Reason rejected |
| :---- | :---- |
| Five separate RDS instances | Cost, ops burden, and FK complexity outweigh benefits at prototype scale |
| Single monolithic schema | No logical service boundaries; violates microservice ownership model |
| Shared schema, no roles | Cannot enforce isolation; unacceptable for multi-service architecture |

### **3.3.2 ADR-002: Schema Boundaries for ETL Persistence**  {#3.3.2-adr-002:-schema-boundaries-for-etl-persistence}

**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** July 2026  
**Deciders:** Group 25

**Context**  
The Ingestion & ETL pipeline processes bulk dealer uploads through AWS Step Functions with a Map state (max concurrency: 10, 100 rows per chunk). The final Load stage must persist validated listings into the Marketplace domain. To adhere to strict microservice architecture principles and prevent cross-schema contamination, direct database writes across service boundaries are prohibited. .

**Decision**  
Enforce strict write isolation across microservices. The Ingestion Service's Load function (loadFn) is restricted strictly to writing within its own ingestion schema (such as updating upload\_jobs and logging stage metrics). Data persistence for listings is encapsulated within the Marketplace domain, ensuring that no microservice executes direct write operations on tables belonging to another service schema. .

**Consequences** 

● **Positive:** 100% strict microservice write isolation is maintained; domain boundaries and data ownership remain clear and uncompromised; eliminates tight schema coupling between Ingestion and Marketplace. 

● **Negative:** Requires an encapsulated handling mechanism for moving data across service domains. 

● **Mitigation:** Idempotent Load logic (FR-41) ensures reprocessing safety, and ETL-loaded listings correctly enter a pending\_review status before becoming visible to users (FR-43). 

**Alternatives Considered** 

| Alternative | Reason rejected |
| :---- | :---- |
| Cross-schema write grant (MarketplaceVehiclesWriteAdapter)  | Violates strict microservice data isolation and service ownership boundaries.  |
| Synchronous HTTP API per row/chunk during Load  | Adds network latency and failure modes under high Map concurrency.  |

### **3.3.3 ADR-003: Step Functions Orchestration over Monolithic ETL Lambda** {#3.3.3-adr-003:-step-functions-orchestration-over-monolithic-etl-lambda}

**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** July 2026  
**Deciders:** Group 25

**Context**  
An earlier design used a single SQS-triggered ETLWorker Lambda to process entire uploads. This approach hit AWS Lambda's 15-minute timeout, could not size memory per task (embedding vs. image processing vs. rule-based parsing), and required hand-written retry and completion tracking.

**Decision**  
Replace the monolithic worker with an AWS Step Functions state machine orchestrating eleven purpose-specific Lambda functions per upload job. Stages pass S3 object keys between states (never inline row data) to respect Step Functions' 256 KB state payload limit. The state machine uses a Map state for parallel chunk processing (MaxConcurrency: 10\) and a Parallel state for concurrent row-processing and image-processing branches.

**Consequences** 

● **Positive:** Declarative Retry/Catch per stage; independent memory sizing (e.g., embed function at 3008 MB, images function at 2048 MB); live execution graph in AWS Console; a failed Groq step degrades one chunk rather than killing the entire upload.

● **Negative:** More Lambda functions to maintain (\~61 invocations per 1,000-row upload vs. \~10 for a fused worker); higher total invocation count.

● **Mitigation:** Shared NestJS module structure across ETL handlers; etl\_stage\_logs table records per-stage status for observability.

**Alternatives Considered** 

| Alternative | Reason rejected |
| :---- | :---- |
| Single monolithic ETL Lambda | Timeout and memory constraints; poor retry granularity |
| ECS/Fargate long-running worker | Outside Free Tier budget; ops overhead |
| SQS-only fan-out without Step Functions | No declarative orchestration; manual completion tracking |

### **3.3.4 ADR-004: Rules-First Normalization with Groq LLM Fallback** {#3.3.4-adr-004:-rules-first-normalization-with-groq-llm-fallback}

**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** July 2026  
**Deciders:** Group 25

**Context**  
Dealer-uploaded inventory data is frequently messy: typos in make/model, abbreviated prices ("8.5m"), inconsistent fuel type spellings. A pure LLM approach would be costly, rate-limit sensitive, and prone to hallucinated values. A pure rules approach fails on genuinely ambiguous rows.

**Decision**  
Apply a deterministic rule-based parser first (dictionary lookups, regex, pg\_trgm fuzzy matching). Calculate a per-field confidence score and a row-level confidence score (minimum of required field scores, never an average). Rows scoring below 0.6 are routed to a dedicated Groq Lambda for LLM-based normalization of unresolved fields only. All LLM outputs pass a whitelist validation layer before merge. If Groq is unavailable, the pipeline proceeds with rules-only results (FR-42.1).

The same rules-first structure applies to natural-language search parsing in the Marketplace Service (FR-21), with a shared normalize library ensuring vocabulary parity between ingestion and search (FR-22.1, NFR-26.1).

**Consequences** 

● **Positive:** Majority of rows processed at zero LLM cost; blast radius of AI errors is bounded to low-confidence fields; graceful degradation on Groq outage.

● **Negative:** Groq is the single non-AWS dependency; free-tier rate limits require Retry/Catch and fallback logic.

● **Mitigation:** Recurring Groq corrections are promoted to vehicle\_dictionaries.aliases (FR-21.4), reducing future LLM calls.

**Alternatives Considered** 

| Alternative | Reason rejected |
| :---- | :---- |
| LLM-first for all rows | Cost, rate limits, hallucination risk |
| Rules-only, no LLM | Fails on ambiguous dealer data (see SRS Appendix B sample row 2\) |
| Per-field HTTP call to Marketplace dictionary API during ETL | Latency under Map concurrency |

### **3.3.5 ADR-005: Internal API Gateway for East-West Service Communication** {#3.3.5-adr-005:-internal-api-gateway-for-east-west-service-communication}

**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** July 2026  
**Deciders:** Group 25

**Context**  
Some operations require one service to invoke another (e.g., Admin approving a dealer must update auth.dealer\_profiles). Direct Lambda-to-Lambda invocation works in AWS but diverges from the local Docker Compose development environment, where services communicate over HTTP.

**Decision**

All service-to-service (east-west) calls will be done via an internal API Gateway or Application Load Balancer using regular HTTP calls. There is consistency in the URL pattern and structure of the request whether you are in local development mode or on AWS. Admin Service calls Auth Service for approve/reject of the dealer; Auth Service does the write in their schema. Admin Service writes to their own admin.audit\_logs table.

North-south traffic (browser to backend) continues through the public API Gateway.

**Consequences** 

● **Positive:** Identical code paths in local and cloud environments; no direct cross-schema writes for admin actions; consistent HTTP semantics and error handling.

● **Negative:** Additional network hop and infrastructure component; internal gateway must be secured (VPC, no public exposure).

● **Mitigation:** Internal gateway is private; JWT validation on all internal routes; least-privilege IAM per Lambda.

**Alternatives Considered** 

| Alternative | Reason rejected |
| :---- | :---- |
| Direct Lambda invocation | Different code path in Docker Compose vs. AWS |
| Admin writes directly to auth schema | Second cross-schema write exception; violates isolation |
| Shared database, no service APIs | Removes service boundaries entirely |

### **3.3.6 ADR-006: Tiered Dealer Onboarding (Individual vs. Business)** {#3.3.6-adr-006:-tiered-dealer-onboarding-(individual-vs.-business)}

**Status:** Accepted  
**Date:** July 2026  
**Deciders:** Group 25

**Context**  
The platform serves both casual individual sellers and registered dealerships. Requiring business registration documents from every seller would exclude legitimate individual sellers. Granting bulk CSV/ZIP upload to unverified individuals would invite abuse and data quality problems.

**Decision**  
Dealers declare a type at registration: **Individual** or **Business**. Verification requirements and platform capabilities scale with tier:

| Tier | Required documents | Capabilities after approval |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Individual | NIC (National Identity Card) | Manual listing creation; capped active listings (configurable limit) |
| Business | Business registration certificate (+ optional signatory NIC) | Uncapped bulk CSV/JSON/ZIP upload via Ingest API |

All dealer registrations enter verification\_status \= pending until an Administrator approves (FR-02). Bulk upload intake (Use Case 4.1.2) requires an authenticated JWT and an approved **Business-tier** profile.

**Consequences** 

● **Positive:** proportionate verification burden; bulk upload gated behind business documentation; aligns with real marketplace trust models.

● **Negative:** SRS FR-26 currently states any Dealer may upload \-  **SRS must be updated** to reflect Business-tier restriction, or FR-26 must be annotated with tier precondition.

● **Mitigation:** Ingest API validates dealer tier from JWT claims or a scoped read of auth.dealer\_profiles before accepting upload.

**Alternatives Considered** 

| Alternative | Reason rejected |
| :---- | :---- |
| Single verification path for all dealers | Over-burdens individuals or under-protects bulk upload |
| No tier distinction | Cannot gate bulk upload meaningfully |

## **3.4	Security Architecture** {#3.4-security-architecture}

This subsection expands the security considerations referenced in Section 11 (Quality) and SRS Section 3.4 (NFR-13 through NFR-20). It describes how authentication, authorization, secrets, and infrastructure permissions are applied across the deployment topology.

### **3.4.1 Authentication Model** {#3.4.1-authentication-model}

The system uses **stateless JWT-based authentication** with revocable refresh tokens (FR-03, FR-04, FR-05, NFR-13).

 

| Token | Purpose | Storage | Lifetime |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Access token | API authorization | Client memory (not localStorage for XSS mitigation where possible) | Short-lived (e.g., 15 minutes) |
| Refresh token | Obtain new access token without re-login | HttpOnly cookie or secure client store | Longer-lived (e.g., 7 days) |

   
**Login flow:** 

1\. Client submits email/password to Auth Service via public API Gateway. 

2\. Auth Service verifies salted password hash (FR-07). 

3\. On success, issues JWT access token (with role claim: buyer, dealer, admin) and refresh token. 

4\. Refresh token hash stored in auth.refresh\_tokens; raw token never persisted (FR-05).

**Token validation:**  
 All HTTP-facing Lambdas validate JWT locally against a shared public key distributed via environment/SSM, avoiding a per-request network call to Auth Service (except for explicit token introspection if added later).

![][image2]

***Figure 02: Authentication sequence \-  login, refresh, and logout. The browser sends credentials to the Auth Service via the API Gateway. On success, short-lived access tokens and longer-lived refresh tokens are issued. Refresh tokens are validated server-side and can be revoked on logout.***

**![][image3]**

### ***Figure 03: Authentication sequence \-  protected API call. The browser sends a request with an access token through the API Gateway to the target service. The service verifies the token locally; if valid, it fetches data and returns the resource. If invalid, the client receives an access-denied response. The Auth Service is not called on every request.*** {#figure-03:-authentication-sequence---protected-api-call.-the-browser-sends-a-request-with-an-access-token-through-the-api-gateway-to-the-target-service.-the-service-verifies-the-token-locally;-if-valid,-it-fetches-data-and-returns-the-resource.-if-invalid,-the-client-receives-an-access-denied-response.-the-auth-service-is-not-called-on-every-request.}

### **3.4.2 Authorization Model (RBAC)** {#3.4.2-authorization-model-(rbac)}

Authorization is enforced via **role-based access control** at the NestJS controller level using RolesGuard (NFR-14). Each user holds exactly one role (FR-08).

 

| Role | Key permissions | Restrictions |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Guest | Browse catalogue; filter/NL search (FR-55) | Cannot save favourites (FR-56); cannot upload |
| Buyer | Search; favourites; profile (FR-16, FR-17, FR-10) | Cannot upload or administer |
| Dealer | Manage own listings; upload (Business tier); poll job status (FR-57–FR-59) | Cannot access admin routes; cannot modify other dealers' data |
| Administrator | User management; upload monitoring; audit logs; reports (FR-44–FR-49) | Cannot self-register (FR-12); actions logged (FR-47) |

**Dealer tier enforcement:**  
 Bulk upload endpoints additionally check dealer\_profiles.dealer\_type \= business and verification\_status \= verified before accepting files (ADR-006).

| Capability | Guest | Buyer | Dealer | Administrator |
| :---- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Browse listings and search | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| Save favourites | **\-**  | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| Manage own profile | **\-**  | **Yes** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| Create and manage own listings | **\-**  | **\-**  | **Yes** | **\-**  |
| Bulk inventory upload | **\-**  | **\-**  | **Business tier\*** | **\-**  |
| View upload job status | **\-**  | **\-**  | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| Verify dealers and manage users | **\-**  | **\-**  | **\-**  | **Yes** |
| View audit logs and reports  | **\-**  | **\-**  | **\-**  | **Yes** |

### **\*bulk upload requires an approved business-tier account**  {#*bulk-upload-requires-an-approved-business-tier-account}

### **3.4.3 Infrastructure Security (IAM)** {#3.4.3-infrastructure-security-(iam)}

Each Lambda function receives a **least-privilege IAM execution role** (NFR-17). Illustrative scoping:

| Lambda / Service | S3 | RDS | SQS | SES | Step Functions | Secrets |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Ingest API | Write raw bucket | Write ingestion schema | Publish | \-  | \-  | Read DB \+ JWT keys |
| ETL load function | Read staging | Write ingestion  | \-  | \-  | \-  | Read DB |
| ETL embed function / images function | Read/write staging | \-  | \-  | \-  | \-  | \-  |
| Marketplace HTTP | Read processed images | Read/write marketplace schema | \-  | \-  | \-  | Read DB \+ Groq key |
| Admin HTTP | \-  | Read all schemas (SELECT) | \-  | \-  | \-  | Read DB |
| Notification | \-  | Write notification schema | Consume events | Send | \-  | Read SES config |

No Lambda receives \* permissions on production resources. Groq API key stored in Secrets Manager / SSM (NFR-20); never hard-coded.

### **3.4.4 Data Security** {#3.4.4-data-security}

● **Passwords:** Salted hashes only (FR-07, NFR-15); never logged. 

● **Transport:** All client-backend traffic over HTTPS (NFR-16). 

● **Vehicle images:** Not publicly writable; served via **signed S3 URLs** (NFR-19). 

● **Dealer verification documents:** Stored in private S3 prefix (dealer-verification/); lifecycle expiry per data-minimization (Data View Section 9). 

● **Input validation:** All API bodies validated and sanitized (NFR-18); LLM outputs whitelist-validated (FR-21.3, FR-33). 

● **Audit trail:** Sensitive admin actions recorded in admin.audit\_logs with actor identity and timestamp (FR-47). Dealer approval: Admin Service calls Auth API; Admin Service writes the audit record \-  Auth Service does **not** write to admin.audit\_logs directly.

### **3.4.5 External Dependency Security** {#3.4.5-external-dependency-security}

Groq API is the **only non-AWS runtime dependency**. The architecture assumes Groq may be unavailable (rate limits, timeouts, outages). All Groq calls are wrapped in Retry/Catch with rules-only fallback (ADR-004, FR-42.1, NFR-12.1). No dealer or buyer PII is sent to Groq beyond unresolved field values and row descriptions required for normalization (FR-33.5, FR-33.7).

## **3.5 API and Interface Architecture** {#3.5-api-and-interface-architecture}

This section describes the system's external and internal API boundaries, complementing SRS Section 3.9 (Interfaces).

### **3.5.1 Public API Gateway (North-South)** {#3.5.1-public-api-gateway-(north-south)}

All browser-to-backend traffic enters through a single **public Amazon API Gateway** REST endpoint. Routes are prefixed by service domain:

| Route prefix | Target service | Auth required | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| /auth/\* | Auth & User | Mixed (register/login public) | JWT issuance, refresh, dealer registration |
| /marketplace/\* | Marketplace | Mixed (search public) | Listings, search, favourites |
| /ingest/\* | Ingestion & ETL | Dealer (Business, verified) | Upload intake, returns 202 \+ Job ID |
| /jobs/\* | Ingestion & ETL | Dealer | Upload job status polling (FR-32) |
| /admin/\* | Admin | Administrator | Dashboard, users, audit logs, reports |
| /notifications/\* | Notification | Internal/event-driven | Not browser-facing in MVP |

**Upload contract (Bulk Upload Intake):** 

● Request: POST /ingest/upload \-  multipart CSV/JSON \+ ZIP 

● Success response: 202 Accepted \+ { jobId: uuid } (FR-31) 

● Failure (format check): 400 Bad Request \+ plain-language reason; no job created 

● Client polls: GET /jobs/{jobId} until status is completed or failed

### **3.5.2 Internal API Gateway (East-West)** {#3.5.2-internal-api-gateway-(east-west)}

Service-to-service calls use a **private internal API Gateway / ALB** (ADR-005):

 

| Caller | Callee | Endpoint (illustrative) | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Admin Service | Auth Service | POST /internal/dealers/{id}/approve | Dealer verification approval |
| Admin Service | Auth Service | POST /internal/dealers/{id}/reject | Dealer verification rejection |
| Admin Service | Auth Service | POST /internal/users/{id}/deactivate | Account deactivation (FR-11) |

   
Internal routes require a valid Administrator JWT or a service-to-service credential (implementation choice: mTLS or signed service token, document chosen approach at implementation time).

### **3.5.3 Asynchronous Interfaces** {#3.5.3-asynchronous-interfaces}

| From | To | Mechanism | Payload |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Ingest API | Step Functions | SQS message | { jobId: uuid } |
| Step Functions | ETL Lambdas | Task state invocation | S3 key references |
| ETL pipeline | Notification Service | Event (via notify function or EventBridge) | Job summary counts |
| Notification Service | Amazon SES | AWS SDK | Rendered email |

Dealer job status uses **polling** (FR-32, Section 3.9.4); no WebSocket in MVP.

## **3.6 Error Handling and Resilience** {#3.6-error-handling-and-resilience}

### **3.6.1 ETL Pipeline Resilience** {#3.6.1-etl-pipeline-resilience}

| Failure type | Handling | SRS / ADR reference |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Groq rate limit / timeout / malformed JSON | Retry with backoff; fall back to rules-only normalization for affected rows | FR-42.1, ADR-004 |
| Row fails validation after rules \+ AI | Write to ingestion.rejected\_records with reason; continue processing chunk | FR-42.2, FR-34 |
| Transient Lambda / network failure | Step Functions Retry with exponential backoff | FR-42, NFR-06 |
| Repeated SQS processing failure | Route to Dead-Letter Queue | FR-42.3 |
| Duplicate SQS delivery | Idempotent Load logic keyed on upload job \+ row identity | FR-41 |
| Entire chunk failure | Other chunks continue independently (Map state isolation) | Section 6.1 Process View |

   
**Graceful degradation example:** A 1,000-row upload during Groq outage completes at \~95% success (rules-only normalization), with incomplete rows in rejected\_records rather than total batch failure (Section 11.1).

### **3.6.2 Search Resilience** {#3.6.2-search-resilience}

| Failure type | Handling | Reference |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Groq unavailable during NL search | Proceed with rules-parsed filters only; skip semantic ranking if no semantic text remains | NFR-12.1, FR-24 |
| Query resolves entirely to structured filters | Skip vector embedding; order by price/date | NFR-12.1 |
| Semantic ranking unavailable | Fall back to filter \+ pg\_trgm search | FR-24 |
| Zero results after full parse | Automated relaxation: widen numeric ranges or drop non-essential filters before empty state | Section 4.1.4 |

### **3.6.3 Notification Resilience** {#3.6.3-notification-resilience}

Notification Service retries transient SES failures without duplicate-sending a notification that already succeeded (FR-54). Delivery status recorded in notification.notifications (FR-53).

*Figure 04: Per-row normalization, Groq fallback, and rejected-record handling.*

## **3.7 CI/CD and Environment Architecture** {#3.7-ci/cd-and-environment-architecture}

### **3.7.1 Repository Structure** {#3.7.1-repository-structure}

| Repository | Deployable unit | Primary artifact |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| auth-user-service | Auth Lambda(s) | Docker image \-\> ECR |
| marketplace-service | Marketplace Lambda(s) | Docker image \-\> ECR |
| ingestion-service | Ingest API \+ 11 ETL Lambdas | Docker image(s) \-\> ECR |
| admin-service | Admin Lambda(s) | Docker image \-\> ECR |
| notification-service | Notification Lambda(s) | Docker image \-\> ECR |
| web-frontend | React SPA | Static build \-\> S3 \+ CloudFront |
| cloud-infrastructure | Terraform modules | AWS resources |
| database/ (folder or repo) | Migrations | SQL migration scripts |

   
Database migrations are **centralized** (Implementation View Section 8.1) because one physical RDS instance holds cross-schema foreign keys.

### **3.7.2 CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions)** {#3.7.2-ci/cd-pipeline-(github-actions)}

![][image6]  
*Figure 06 :Row-level ETL error handling. Each upload row is normalized with rules first; low-confidence rows use Groq with retry and rules-only fallback. Valid rows are loaded; invalid rows are saved to rejected\_records and processing continues*

Typical pipeline stages per service repository:

1\. **Lint & typecheck** : ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript (NFR-21) 

2\. **Unit tests** : Jest; minimum coverage target per NFR-23 

3\. **Build** : Docker image for Lambda handlers 

4\. **Push** : Amazon ECR 

5\. **Deploy** : Update Lambda function image/tag via Terraform or AWS CLI 

6\. **Integration tests** (optional post-deploy) : smoke test against dev environment

Infrastructure changes flow through cloud-infrastructure Terraform plan/apply, never manual AWS Console changes (SRS Section 2.4, NFR-30).

### **3.7.3 Environments** {#3.7.3-environments}

 

| Environment | Purpose | Constraints |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Local (Docker Compose) | Developer testing | Internal HTTP between services; local Postgres or RDS dev instance |
| AWS Dev / Demo | Integration, UAT, viva demo | Free Tier limits; single RDS, single region |
| Production (future) | Not in MVP scope | Would add multi-AZ RDS, WAF, separate accounts |

   
Local development mirrors east-west HTTP via Docker Compose service names, matching ADR-005.

## **3.8 Testing Architecture** {#3.8-testing-architecture}

This section describes the **architectural approach to testing**, not a detailed test plan. Testing validates that each architectural boundary (service, schema, pipeline stage) behaves as specified in the SRS.

### **3.8.1 Testing Layers** {#3.8.1-testing-layers}

| Layer | Scope | Tools / approach |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Unit | Individual services, parsers, confidence scoring, adapters | Jest; mock repositories and AWS SDK adapters |
| Integration | Service \+ PostgreSQL; Service \+ S3; ETL stage handlers | Test containers or dedicated test schema; LocalStack for S3/SQS where feasible |
| Pipeline | End-to-end ETL: upload \-\> normalize \-\> embed \-\> load \-\> pending\_review | Step Functions local or dev AWS; fixture CSV/ZIP files (SRS Appendix B) |
| End-to-end | Browser \-\> API Gateway \-\> full upload \+ search flow | Playwright or Cypress against dev deployment |
| Search quality | NL parser accuracy; embedding consistency | Fixture queries; assert FR-22.1 model parity |

 

### **3.8.2 Architecturally Significant Test Cases** {#3.8.2-architecturally-significant-test-cases}

● **ADR-002:** Load adapter writes only to marketplace.vehicles and vehicle\_images; DELETE attempt fails at DB grant level. 

● **ADR-004:** Row with confidence ≥ 0.6 never invokes Groq; row below 0.6 does; Groq outage falls back to rules-only. 

● **ADR-006:** Individual dealer receives 403 on bulk upload endpoint; Business verified dealer receives 202\. 

● **FR-41:** Reprocessing same SQS message does not create duplicate listings. 

● **FR-43:** ETL-loaded listing has status \= pending\_review; not returned in public search until dealer approves. 

● **FR-22.1:** Query embedding model matches listing embedding model (same library version).

 

### **3.8.3 Test Data** {#3.8.3-test-data}

SRS Section 2.2 uses an artificial vehicle data generation tool that allows tests without any dealer data. Tests fixtures comply with SRS Appendix B (clean row \+ dirty row) and are used for validating deterministic parser vs. Groq fall-back paths.

4. # **Use-Case View**  {#use-case-view}

The following use cases describe the important architectural features of the system. Each one uses more than one service and/or a delicate architectural component (asynchronous processing, hybrid search ranking, or human review gate).

### **Guest Use Cases** {#guest-use-cases}

The guest interacts with the system through the public-facing web frontend without requiring authentication.

| Use Case | Brief Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Register** | Allows the guest to create a new account to become an authenticated Buyer or Dealer. |
| **Search Vehicles** | Allows the guest to search the marketplace using traditional UI filters or free-text natural language queries. |
| **View Vehicle Details** | Displays the full specifications, image gallery, and dealer contact information for a specific vehicle listing. |

![][image7]

*Figure 7 : shows the main functions available to an unauthenticated guest. The architecturally significant guest function is the natural-language vehicle search, as it triggers the 5-stage deterministic parser, interacts with the external Groq LLM API for fallback resolution, and queries persistent vector embeddings using PostgreSQL's pgvector* 

### 

### **Buyer Use Cases** {#buyer-use-cases}

The buyer interacts with the system through the authenticated web frontend.

| Use Case | Brief Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Log In** | Authenticates the buyer and provides a JWT for access to secured application features. |
| **Search Vehicles** | Allows the buyer to search listings using structured UI filters or natural language, extending the guest capability. |
| **View Vehicle Details** | Displays the full vehicle information and dealer details. |
| **View Recommendations** | Displays semantically related vehicle listings based on vector similarity. |
| **Manage Profile** | Allows the buyer to view and update their personal profile information. |
| **Manage Favourites** | Allows the buyer to save specific vehicle listings to a personal list and remove them as needed. |

![][image8]

*Figure 8 : the functions available to a buyer. The "Manage Favourites" and "View Recommendations" use cases have significant architectural coverage, as they bridge authentication boundaries, require foreign-key interactions between the auth and marketplace database schemas, and heavily utilize semantic similarity calculations.*

### **Dealer Use Cases** {#dealer-use-cases}

The dealer interacts with the system primarily through the authenticated dealer dashboard on the web frontend.

| Use Case | Brief Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Register** | Submits a dealer registration request, which is placed in a pending state until approved by an Administrator. |
| **Log In** | Authenticates the dealer and provides access to inventory management functions. |
| **Upload Inventory** | Allows the dealer to perform a bulk upload using a CSV/JSON file alongside a ZIP archive of vehicle images. |
| **View Dashboard** | Displays an overview of the dealer's active inventory, upload history, and profile status. |
| **Track Upload Status** | Allows the dealer to monitor the progress of active bulk upload jobs and view row-level validation errors. |
| **Manage Listings** | Allows the dealer to edit details, deactivate live listings, and explicitly review/confirm any data that was automatically generated by the LLM (Pending Review status). |
| **Receive Notifications** | Delivers asynchronous email alerts to the dealer regarding the success or failure of their bulk upload jobs. |

![][image9]

*Figure 9 : details the functions available to a dealer. Inventory upload and listing management are the most architecturally complex operations in the system. They orchestrate the 11-Lambda AWS Step Functions ETL pipeline, handle distributed file processing via Amazon S3 and SQS, enforce human-in-the-loop AI validation, and execute the system's single cross-schema write exception into the marketplace.vehicles table.*

### **Administrator Use Cases** {#administrator-use-cases}

The administrator uses a secured administrative web dashboard to manage institution-level information, user statuses, and overall platform health.

| Use Case | Brief Description |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Log In** | Authenticates the administrator and provides access to system-wide administrative functions. |
| **Review Audit Logs** | Allows the administrator to review chronological records of sensitive system and administrative actions. |
| **Monitor Upload Jobs** | Displays the status and metrics of all ETL upload jobs occurring across the entire platform. |
| **View Reports** | Provides platform-level analytical summaries regarding total listings, user activity, and ETL error rates. |
| **Manage Users** | Allows the administrator to view all user accounts, approve pending dealer registrations, and suspend or reactivate profiles. |

![][image10]

*Figure 10:  shows the administrative functions required to oversee the platform. Dashboard reporting and monitoring use cases are architecturally significant because they exercise the system's admin\_service\_role database isolation exception, safely executing cross-schema read queries to aggregate data from the auth, marketplace, and ingestion schemas without compromising strict microservice write boundaries.*

1. ## **Use-Case Realizations** {#use-case-realizations}

The following realizations describe selected use cases that exercise several architectural elements or represent operationally important workflows. Supporting activity, sequence, and state diagrams for these realizations are presented later in the Process View. 

#### **4.1.1 Register and Tiered Authorization**

| Use case name | Register and Tiered Authorization |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Actor(s)** | Guest, Dealer, Administrator |
| **Description** | A Guest registers as a Dealer, selecting a specific tier (Individual or Business) and uploading required documentation. An Administrator reviews the application, unlocking tier-specific platform capabilities upon approval. |
| **Preconditions** | The supplied email address is not associated with an existing account. The required document (NIC for Individual; Business Registration Certificate for Business) is provided. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The Guest submits registration details, selects a dealer type, and uploads the required documentation via the frontend. 2\. The Auth-User Service hashes the password and stores the uploaded documents in a private Amazon S3 prefix (dealer-verification/). 3\. The service creates a new dealer\_profiles record in PostgreSQL (auth schema) with a pending verification status. 4\. An Administrator reviews the uploaded documents via the secure Admin dashboard. 5\. The Administrator approves the application. 6\. The Auth-User Service updates the database status to verified, logs the decision to audit\_logs, and unlocks platform capabilities based on the dealer type (manual listing limits for Individual; bulk upload access for Business). 7\. The dealer is notified of the approval via email. |
| **Successful end/post condition** | A verified dealer\_profiles row exists, tier-specific platform capabilities are unlocked, and the client holds a valid JWT with appropriate role claims. |
| **Fail end/post condition** | If the Administrator rejects the application, the status becomes rejected, the reason is logged, and the dealer is notified to resubmit corrected documents. |
| **Contributing design elements** | Auth-User Service, Amazon S3, PostgreSQL (auth schema), Notification Service (Amazon SES). |

#### **4.1.2 Bulk Upload Intake**

| Use case name | Bulk Upload Intake |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Actor(s)** | Dealer |
| **Description** | A verified Business Dealer submits a CSV/JSON inventory file and a ZIP of vehicle images. The system stores the raw files and starts asynchronous processing without blocking the dealer's request. |
| **Preconditions** | The Dealer is authenticated, possesses a valid JWT, and has an approved Business-tier profile. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The Dealer submits the CSV/JSON file and image ZIP via the frontend. 2\. The Ingest API (Ingestion and ETL Service) verifies the JWT locally against a shared public key, avoiding a network call to the Auth Service. 3\. The API performs a format-only check (validating it is parseable CSV/JSON and a real ZIP archive). 4\. The API streams the raw files, untouched, directly into Amazon S3. 5\. The API creates an upload\_jobs row in PostgreSQL (ingestion schema) with a PENDING status. 6\. The API publishes exactly one message containing the Job ID to an Amazon SQS queue. 7\. The API immediately responds to the frontend with a 202 Accepted HTTP status and the Job ID. |
| **Successful end/post condition** | An upload\_jobs record exists with status PENDING, raw files are durably stored in S3, and the payload is queued in SQS awaiting Step Functions execution. |
| **Fail end/post condition** | If the files fail the format-only check, the request is rejected synchronously with a clear reason, and no job or queue message is created. |
| **Contributing design elements** | Ingestion and ETL Service, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, PostgreSQL (ingestion schema).  |

### 

### 

### **4.1.3 Process and Review Pending Listings** {#4.1.3-process-and-review-pending-listings}

| Use case name | Process and Review Pending Listings |
| :---- | :---- |
| Actor(s) | Dealer |
| Description | Following a bulk upload, an automated ETL pipeline orchestrates the chunking, normalization, and embedding of data using targeted AWS Lambda functions. All accepted rows are persisted as PENDING\_REVIEW listings. The Dealer then completes the use case by explicitly reviewing and confirming any AI-inferred data before the listings are published. |
| Preconditions | The Dealer has successfully initiated the "Bulk Upload Intake" use case, and the asynchronous AWS Step Functions execution is underway. |
| Main flow | 1\. The validateFile function Lambda checks headers and file integrity once for the entire file. 2\. The splitChunks function Lambda divides the file into 100-row chunks, passing S3 descriptor pointers to a parallel Map state. 3\. Inside the Map state, the parseNormalize function Lambda applies a 6-step normalizer to each field and calculates a row-level confidence score. 4\. If the confidence score is \< 0.6, the groqNormalize function Lambda routes unresolved fields to the external Groq API (LLM) for contextual inference, subsequently dropping any hallucinated values. 5\. The validateRows function Lambda validates mandatory business rules; rows failing this step are written to rejected\_records. 6\. The enrich function Lambda maps JSONB specifications based on vehicle type and builds the final search\_text. 7\. The embed function Lambda generates a 384-dimensional vector embedding using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model. 8\. The Load function Lambda executes a bulk-insert, saving accepted rows into the marketplace.vehicles table with a PENDING\_REVIEW status. 9\. The Dealer opens the dashboard, reviews the AI-inferred fields, and confirms the data, transitioning the listing status to LIVE. |
| Successful end/post condition | Valid rows exist as LIVE searchable listings, rejected rows are recorded with actionable reasons, and the dealer has explicitly confirmed all AI-inferred data. |
| Fail end/post condition | If the Groq API is unavailable, the pipeline catches the error and proceeds to validation using rules-only data, degrading gracefully rather than failing the entire batch. |
| Contributing design elements | AWS Step Functions, ETL Lambdas (validateFile function, splitChunks function, parseNormalize function, groqNormalize function, validateRows function, enrich function, embed function, Load function), Amazon S3, Groq API, PostgreSQL, Marketplace Service. |

#### **4.1.4 Intelligent Search Execution**

| Use case name | Intelligent Search Execution |
| ----- | ----- |
| **Actor(s)** | Buyer, Guest |
| **Description** | A user searches the marketplace using a free-text natural-language query. The system utilizes a 5-stage deterministic parser, an LLM fallback, and semantic embeddings to return a highly accurate, ranked result list. |
| **Preconditions** | None. The feature is available to both authenticated Buyers and unauthenticated Guests. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The user submits a free-text query via the frontend search bar. 2\. The Marketplace Service tokenizes the query, masks stopwords, and executes Stage 1 (Multi-word phrase extraction) and Stage 2 (Numeric pattern extraction). 3\. The service executes Stage 3 (Exact Dictionary Hits) and Stage 4 (Fuzzy dictionary hits via pg\_trgm), strictly resolving Make before Model. 4\. The service calculates a confidence score based on coverage and numeric signals. 5\. If the confidence score is \< 0.6, unresolved tokens and a shortlist of candidates are sent to the Groq API for LLM-assisted filter extraction. 6\. All returned LLM fields are strictly whitelist-validated against the database schema. 7\. The service passes the remaining unconsumed semantic text to the embedding library to produce a query vector. 8\. The service executes a single PostgreSQL query combining exact filter conditions (WHERE clauses) and pgvector semantic ranking (ORDER BY embedding \<=\> vector). 9\. Ranked, paginated results are returned to the user. |
| **Successful end/post condition** | A ranked list of matching listings is returned, and a record is logged in the search\_queries table to fuel future alias promotion. |
| **Fail end/post condition** | If the query returns zero results, the system executes an automated relaxation path (widening numeric ranges or dropping non-essential filters) before returning an empty state. |
| **Contributing design elements** | Marketplace Service, Groq API, PostgreSQL (marketplace schema, utilizing pg\_trgm and pgvector). |

### **4.1.5 Monitor Platform Activity and Audit Logs** {#4.1.5-monitor-platform-activity-and-audit-logs}

| Use case name | Monitor Platform Activity and Audit Logs |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Actor(s)** | Administrator |
| **Description** | The Administrator logs into the web dashboard to monitor upload jobs across the platform, review system audit logs, and view aggregate reports. This scenario exercises the system's cross-schema read architecture, allowing the Admin Service to aggregate data securely across microservice boundaries. |
| **Preconditions** | The Administrator is authenticated with a valid JWT containing Administrator role claims. |
| **Main flow** | 1\. The Administrator requests the platform dashboard view via the frontend. 2\. The API Gateway routes the request to the Admin Service. 3\. The Admin Service utilizes the admin\_service\_role database user to execute authorized cross-schema SELECT queries across the isolated auth, marketplace, and ingestion schemas. 4\. The Admin Service retrieves aggregate bulk upload statuses and metrics directly from the ingestion.upload\_jobs table. 5\. The Admin Service retrieves records of sensitive system actions from its own admin.audit\_logs table. 6\. The Admin Service retrieves total active listing metrics from the marketplace.vehicles table. 7\. The service formats the aggregated data and returns it to the client to populate the dashboard tiles. |
| **Successful end/post condition** | The Administrator receives an accurate, real-time aggregate view of platform activity, and the system successfully executes cross-schema reads without violating write-isolation rules. |
| **Fail end/post condition** | An unauthorized request (e.g., a Dealer attempting to access the route) is intercepted by role-based guards and rejected with a 403 Forbidden status, returning no data. |
| **Contributing design elements** | Admin Service, PostgreSQL (specifically utilizing the admin\_service\_role cross-schema SELECT grants). |

5. # **Logical View**  {#logical-view}

   1. ## **Overview** {#overview-1}

This architecture splits into five independently deployable services and one shared library layer. Each of the services is designed to use the same internal package structure (config, common, infrastructure, modules, health, lambda). So that each team member can move through each service easily. The domain logic resides in the modules/{feature}/{controllers,services,repositories,entities,dto} layer while the usage of the AWS SDK is done from infrastructure/adapters layer only.

* **auth-user-service** :  registration (including tiered Individual/Business dealer verification), login, JWT/refresh tokens, roles, dealer approval.

* **marketplace-service :** listings, favourites, filter/NL/semantic/trigram search, recommendations, and the shared vehicle\_dictionaries reference table (makes/models/fuel/transmission) used for trigram matching.

* **ingestion-service :** the Ingest API, Job Status API, and the eleven-Lambda Step Functions ETL pipeline.

* **admin-service :** user management, upload monitoring, reports, audit logs.

* **notification-service :** event-driven SES email notifications.

* **shared normalize \+ embed library :** the dictionaries, regex rules, and MiniLM embedding wrapper used by bo

* the marketplace-service (query-side) and ingestion-service (listing-side), per the model-parity constraint in Section 3\.

![][image11]

*Figure 11 : Backend module packages and documented cross-module dependencies (shared RDS, modular monolith).*

2. ## **Architecturally Significant Design Packages** {#architecturally-significant-design-packages}

**5.2.1 Auth & User \- auth module**

* **AuthController :** login/refresh/logout HTTP entrypoints,  plus dealer registration (including document upload) entrypoints.

* **AuthService :**credential verification, JWT issuance, orchestrates RefreshTokenService; for Dealer registration, captures the selected dealer\_type and stores verification document references via DealerProfilesRepository.

* **RefreshTokenService :** issues, validates, and revokes refresh tokens (hashed at rest).

* **JwtStrategy / RolesGuard :** Passport JWT validation and RBAC enforcement used by every service.

* **DealerApprovalService :** transitions dealer\_profiles.is\_verified through pending/verified/rejected; exposed to admin-service via the internal API Gateway/ALB rather than a direct database write from Admin.

* **DealerProfilesRepository :** persists dealer\_type, business fields, verification\_documents, and is\_verified state; written by AuthService at registration and by DealerApprovalService at approval/rejection.

![][image12]

**Figure 12: auth- user class diagram**

**5.2.2 Marketplace \- search module**

* **SearchController :** exposes filter, natural-language, and combined search endpoints.

* **DeterministicParser :** extracts structured filters from free text (shared logic family with the ingestion parser, per the ETL design's "same rules-first structure" principle).

* **PgvectorSearchAdapter / TrigramSearchAdapter :** thin infrastructure-layer wrappers around the respective PostgreSQL extensions.

* **SearchService :** merges filter, vector, and trigram results into one ranked response and applies the semantic-search fallback.

* **VehicleDictionariesRepository :** owns the vehicle\_dictionaries reference table (canonical makes/models/fuel/transmission values plus alias history); read directly by ingestion-service via a scoped grant and cached in memory at container init.

![][image13]

**Figure 13 : Marketplace class diagram**

**5.2.3 Ingestion & ETL \- pipeline package (src/workers/etl-worker/pipeline/)**

* **normalize/ :**  ParseNormalizeHandler (rules, confidence scoring) and GroqNormalizeHandler (LLM fallback, flagged rows only).

* **validate/ :** ValidateFileHandler (whole-file structural checks) and ValidateRowsHandler (per-row mandatory-field checks).

*  **enrich/ :** EnrichHandler (derived fields, JSONB attributes, search\_text construction).

*  **embeddings/ :** EmbedHandler (MiniLM inference, loaded at module scope for warm-container reuse).

* **image-processing/ :**  ImagesHandler (Sharp resize/compress, registration-number keyed matching to rows).

* **persistence/ : MarketplaceVehiclesWriteAdapter \-** the only class with the scope and column-based granting of ingestion\_service\_role in marketplace.vehicles; plain parameterized SQL and not an import of shared entity classes, in order to keep the domain models of the two services separate. This is the only intentional exception to write ownership by each service (see Goal 3 in Cross-service data isolation model from Section 3 for more details); restricting it to only one named class ensures that any such future write to another schema will stand out in the diffs. 

**![][image14]**

*Figure 14 : Ingestion class diagram*

**5.2.4 Admin \- modules**

* **UserManagementService, ReportService, AuditLogService, DashboardService :** as scoped in the SRS's FR-43 through FR-48.

![][image15]

*Figure 15 : Admin class diagram*

**5.2.5 Notification \- notifications module**

* **NotificationEventHandler, EmailTemplateService, SesAdapter :**  as scoped in FR-49 through FR-53.

6. # **Process View**  {#process-view}

This part explains the process decomposition in terms of lightweight and heavyweight processes (threads of control). It explains the interactions among microservices, the AWS infrastructure, and external APIs to achieve the main use cases for the Second Hand Vehicle Marketplace.

## **6.1 Process Organisation and Communication** {#6.1-process-organisation-and-communication}

The main runtime processes are organized into the following groups:

| Process group | Main participants | Communication |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Dealer Registration & Authentication** | Dealer, React Frontend, API Gateway, Auth-User Service, PostgreSQL (auth schema), Amazon S3 | Synchronous API requests, JWT local validation, and relational database queries. |
| **Bulk Upload Intake** | Dealer, React Frontend, API Gateway, Ingestion API, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS | Synchronous API requests for file ingestion, transitioning to asynchronous message passing via SQS queues. |
| **ETL Chunk Processing** | AWS Step Functions, ETL Lambdas (Normalize, Validate, Enrich, Embed, Load), Groq API, PostgreSQL (marketplace schema) | Orchestrated state machine transitions passing S3 reference keys, synchronous external LLM API calls, and optimized database batch inserts. |
| **Hybrid Natural-Language Search** | Buyer, React Frontend, API Gateway, Marketplace Service, Groq API, PostgreSQL (marketplace schema) | Synchronous API requests, fast in-memory parsing, external LLM fallback via HTTP, and semantic vector database queries. |
| **Administrative Monitoring** | Administrator, Web Dashboard, Admin Service, PostgreSQL (All schemas) | Synchronous authorized API calls executing cross-schema database reads via restricted PostgreSQL roles. |

## 

## 

## **6.2 Bulk Inventory Upload & ETL Orchestration Activity** {#6.2-bulk-inventory-upload-&-etl-orchestration-activity}

![][image17]  
*Figure 17: shows the end-to-end workflow of bulk inventory upload from the perspective of the Dealer, Ingest API, AWS Step Functions, and SQS swimlanes. The dealer uploads a CSV or JSON file that contains data about vehicles together with a ZIP file of vehicle images. As the aim is to provide a synchronous response at a rapid pace, the Ingest API only runs a lightweight validation, keeps the files unmodified in the S3 storage service of Amazon, and kicks off an SQS queue with a message.*

The extraction, transformation, and loading process is controlled by an AWS Step Functions workflow. Initially, the workflow conducts header validation and splits the dataset into chunks. Chunks are processed in parallel using a Map state. In each of the Map states, the system conducts normalization, uses Groq LLM to validate low-confidence fields, validates the data, generates vector embeddings, and inserts data into the database in bulk. Listings that are processed correctly are marked as PENDING\_REVIEW which implies that they have to be confirmed by the dealer. Meanwhile, another branch processes vehicle images and adds them to listings.

## **6.3 Hybrid Natural-Language Search Activity** {#6.3-hybrid-natural-language-search-activity}

![][image18]  
*Figure 18:  describes how a buyer's free-text query is processed by the Marketplace Service. The query is tokenized and passed through a multi-stage deterministic parser that extracts multi-word phrases, numeric patterns, and exact dictionary matches. The parser utilizes pg\_trgm to perform fuzzy similarity matching for large vocabularies like vehicle makes and models.*

In case the parser generates a confidence level that falls short of an acceptable value, the unparseable tokens are sent over to the Groq API to be analyzed using LLMs. The unparseable descriptive words get mapped to the semanticText and converted to a vector with a dimension of 384\. Lastly, a single PostgreSQL query is run to execute the search.

## **6.4 Dealer Registration & Tiered Authorization Sequence** {#6.4-dealer-registration-&-tiered-authorization-sequence}

![][image19]  
*Figure 19: shows how the registration, validation, and authorization for a Dealer are accomplished via the Auth-User service. During registration, the dealer is required to enter a dealer type, which can be either Individual or Business, and provide the required supporting document, which can be NIC and/or Business Registration Certificate. The provided documents are stored in a private bucket on Amazon S3.*

The account gets into the pending mode until the documents get approval by an administrator through the Admin dashboard. Once the documents are approved, the approval is logged into the audit log, and certain features would get unlocked based on the dealer type; individual dealers are able to make manual listings with limited numbers, while business dealers are able to upload listings in bulk through CSV/JSON/ZIP files using Ingest API.

## **6.5 Bulk Upload Intake & SQS Decoupling Sequence** {#6.5-bulk-upload-intake-&-sqs-decoupling-sequence}

![][image20]  
*Figure 20: shows the asynchronous intake boundary covered by the Ingestion and ETL Service. For ensuring that the response time is fast and the process happens in a synchronous manner, the time-consuming task is offloaded to the AWS Step Function state machine.*

The Ingest API just checks if the token from the dealer is JWT or not through the use of the public key, which is done without making any calls to the Auth Service for each individual request. The basic validation for ensuring that the payload has the required format (CSV/JSON in ZIP file) is also performed by the API. The raw files are kept intact on Amazon S3 for being the point of truth. An upload job and one SQS message are created.

## **6.6 ETL Chunk Processing (The Map State) Sequence** {#6.6-etl-chunk-processing-(the-map-state)-sequence}

![][image21]

*Figure 21: represents the Parallel Data Processing Loop in the AWS Step Functions Map State. Due to limitations set by AWS payload size, the state machine operates on an execution-per-upload basis. The SplitIntoChunks step results in a small array of descriptors pointing to row ranges in S3, which is spread out using the Map state up to 10 concurrent executions in order to keep the database connection pool safe.*

Within the Map State, the normalize function parses the normalize function function, and 6-step normalization is performed for each of the fields, while the confidence level for the row is obtained based on the minimum score rule. When the score is less than 0.6, the rows are sent to the Groq API for inference using instruction block and shortlisted makes as candidates. After this, the output is checked through whitelisting, where enrich function produces the JSONB specification for the vehicles based on their type, creating the search\_text. embed function creates the vector using all-MiniLM-L6-v2.

## **6.7 Intelligent Search Execution Sequence** {#6.7-intelligent-search-execution-sequence}

![][image22]

*Figure 22: presents the execution flow of a natural-language search query processed by a deterministic 5-stage parser. The tokenizer lowercases text, strips punctuation, splits words, and masks domain-specific stopwords without deleting them. The parser extracts multi-word phrases and numeric patterns, flagging adjacent tokens as digit-adjacent. It then executes exact dictionary hits, strictly resolving Make before Model. Stage 4 performs fuzzy matching using pg\_trgm for large vocabularies, utilizing type-gating to reject digit-adjacent tokens outright. Unconsumed tokens are routed into semanticText.*

In the case that the confidence score falls below 0.6, the LLM Repair flow kicks in. The LLM fields returned are subject to the Whitelist check no matter what. In case semanticText is not empty, the vector embedding is generated. Finally, the Marketplace service performs a single query using WHERE and ORDER BY clauses.

## **6.8 Dealer Account Verification State** {#6.8-dealer-account-verification-state}

![][image23]

*Figure 23: displays the state progression of a Dealer account within the Auth-User Service schema, illustrating the tiered onboarding process. An account begins as REGISTERED and moves to PENDING\_VERIFICATION once required documentation is uploaded to S3. An Administrator reviews these documents. Approved documents transition the account to a VERIFIED state, unlocking specific capabilities based on the dealer tier (capped manual listings for Individual, bulk ingestion for Business). Denied documents transition the state to REJECTED, requiring the dealer to resubmit. Any verified account may be transitioned to SUSPENDED due to policy violations.*

## **6.9 Vehicle Listing State (Row-Level Lifecycle)** {#6.9-vehicle-listing-state-(row-level-lifecycle)}

![][image24]

*Figure 24: outlines the lifecycle of an individual vehicle listing row as it progresses through the ETL pipeline(AWS State Machine) and into the live marketplace. A listing begins as a raw text row in a CSV file and transitions through PARSED, NORMALIZED, and VALIDATED states as it navigates the 6-step normalizer and business rules. Rows falling below a 0.6 confidence threshold temporarily enter a GROQ\_REPAIR state.*

After enriching the listing with specifications and inserting the vector into it, the Load operation adds the row to the database, thereby moving the listing into a PENDING\_REVIEW state. The listing goes into a LIVE state only when the dealer approves the inferred data by the AI through the dashboard. In case the dealer changes the searchable text in a live listing, the listing will move into a PENDING\_REVIEW state again.

7. # **Deployment View**  {#deployment-view}

The system deploys entirely on AWS. The physical and logical nodes are organized as follows:

* **Client Device:** Runs a modern web browser and loads the React Single Page Application (SPA).  
* **Amazon S3 \+ CloudFront (optional):** Hosts the built React static assets.  
* **Amazon API Gateway (Public):** Serves as the single public entry point, routing north-south HTTPS requests to the correct backend Lambda functions.  
* **Internal API Gateway / ALB (Private):** Routes east-west, service-to-service HTTP calls (e.g., Admin's dealer approve/reject call into Auth). It is kept as plain HTTP rather than direct Lambda invocation so local Docker Compose development and AWS deployment share the same code path (ADR-005).  
* **AWS Lambda:** Executes all backend code. The 5 logical microservices are physically deployed as **18 distinct Lambda functions** to optimize cold starts, memory allocation, and packaging constraints:  
  * **Ingestion & ETL Service (13 Lambdas):** 11 dedicated Lambdas orchestrated by Step Functions for the ETL pipeline, plus 2 asynchronous API Lambdas: ingest-upload-api (handling heavy multi-part file streams) and job-status-api (handling high-frequency, lightweight dashboard polling).  
  * **Marketplace Service (2 Lambdas):** Asymmetrically split into marketplace-api (handling lightweight CRUD and favourites) and search-api (handling the parser, Groq fallback, MiniLM, and pgvector).  
  * **Auth & User Service:** 1 Lambda.  
  * **Admin Service:** 1 Lambda.  
  * **Notification Service:** 1 Lambda.  
* **Lambda Packaging & Dependency Isolation (NFR-27):**  
  * *Heavy Inference/Processing:* Any Lambda loading the heavy all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding model (embed function and search-api) is deployed as an **Amazon ECR Docker Container Image** sized at 1–3 GB. The images function Lambda utilizing the C++ Sharp library is isolated in a \~2048 MB Docker image.  
  * *Lightweight HTTP APIs:* All other HTTP-facing handlers (Auth, Admin, Notification, Marketplace-API, Ingestion-Sync-APIs) and rule-based ETL Lambdas are packaged as **ZIP archives** (or slim Docker images \< 50MB). This explicit separation prevents heavy dependencies from increasing cold-start latency on standard, user-facing API calls.  
* **AWS Step Functions:** The state machine coordinating one execution per upload job across the 11 ETL Lambdas.  
* **Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL \+ pgvector \+ pg\_trgm):** The single shared relational data store, reachable from Lambda functions inside the deployment VPC. Organized as one schema per service with service-specific database roles.  
* **Amazon RDS Proxy:** Connection pooler sitting in front of RDS, required specifically so the ETL Load stage's Map-driven concurrency (MaxConcurrency: 10\) does not open 10 raw connections per upload and exhaust the pool shared with live buyer traffic.  
* **Amazon S3 (Raw and Staging Buckets):** s3://raw/ holds the original, permanent dealer uploads; s3://staging/ holds per-stage intermediate JSON payloads utilized by Step Functions, configured with a \~7-day expiry lifecycle rule.  
* **Amazon SQS:** Durably buffers upload-start messages between the Ingest API and AWS Step Functions.  
* **Amazon SES:** Handles outbound transactional emails for the Notification Service.  
* **Amazon CloudWatch:** Centralizes logs and metrics for all Lambda functions and the Step Functions execution history.  
* **AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store:** Securely stores database credentials and third-party API keys (e.g., the Groq API key).  
* **AWS IAM:** Enforces least-privilege execution roles scoped strictly per Lambda function.

Deployment diagram

8. # **Implementation View**  {#implementation-view}

   1. ## **Overview** {#overview-2}

Source code structure: One repository per deployable unit: auth-user-service, marketplace-service, ingestion-service, admin-service, notification-service, web-frontend, and cloud infrastructure (Terraform). The migrations themselves are kept in one db repository/folder and not in individual services’ repositories since the physical RDS database is shared across the team and there are foreign keys that link services (e.g. vehicles.dealer\_id \-\> foreign key to users.id), thus splitting the migrations into different repositories will reintroduce the order dependency despite the coupling being present in the first place. All services will interact with their own tables within the application code.

Inclusion of layers principle: is applicable to all services. Controller and Lambda Handler are skinny (just request processing); Business Logic is implemented in Services, Database access – in Repositories; AWS SDK can be used only at infrastructure/adapters layer. This is the principle that makes possible independent testing of ETL Lambda Handlers without AWS and database.

**![][image25]**

*Figure 25: component diagram (Layering)* 

2. ## **Layers** {#layers}

| Layer | Contents |
| :---- | :---- |
| Presentation | NestJS controllers (HTTP) and Lambda handler entrypoints (event-triggered); request/response DTO validation only. |
| Application | Services containing business logic \- e.g. SearchService's ranking merge, EnrichHandler's derivation rules, RefreshTokenService's revocation logic. |
| Persistence | Repositories and ORM entities; the only layer permitted to construct SQL/query-builder calls. |
| Infrastructure | AWS SDK adapters \- S3Adapter, SqsAdapter, SesAdapter, StepFunctionsAdapter, GroqClientAdapter \- isolating third-party/AWS API shapes from business logic. |
| Shared/Common | Guards, decorators, DTO base types, and the shared normalize+embed library consumed by both marketplace-service and ingestion-service. |

9. # **Data View (optional)** {#data-view-(optional)}

The system's persistent data includes a single relational database and two S3 buckets.

Only one Amazon RDS database PostgreSQL is present, which makes use of the following extensions for: Users, DealerProfiles, RefreshTokens, UploadJobs, Vehicles (which has a column vector(384) of embedding, tsvector type search\_vector column, and trigram-indexed make/model/description columns), VehicleImages, Favourites, SearchQueries (where the user\_id field is optional to track Guest queries), RejectedRecords, ETLStageLogs, Notifications, and AuditLogs. As part of the initial migration, email uniqueness and JSONB attributes of Vehicle type are made sure to ensure that no future migrations are needed.

Iisolated model: although the instance is physically a shared instance, the logical structure of the schemas is such that each service has its own schema, and each service has its own database role. The reads can access other service schemas through explicitly granted narrow SELECT rights – the admin\_service\_role, for example, has access to marketplace.vehicles and ingestion.upload\_jobs for dashboards and ingestion\_service\_role has access to marketplace.vehicle\_dictionaries. The Writes are strictly isolated to the schema owned by the owning service, with zero exceptions. Every service holds exclusive write privileges over its own tables, ensuring complete data ownership and boundary enforcement 

Dealer profiles distinguish between dealer types with the help of dealer\_type enum (individual, business). Business\_registration\_no, business\_address, and city will be filled if the dealer is of type Business while these fields will remain NULL if the dealer is of type Individual where dealers are distinguished by users.name. Verification documents is a JSONB field consisting of S3 key links to those documents that are actually required (NIC for Individual, business registration certificate for Business along with optional signatory NIC) depending on the specific dealer type, so as to avoid creating partially NULL columns for those documents that are not required for some dealer types, just like in case of vehicles.specs. Verified\_by refers to the Administrator who verified or rejected the request. Documents are stored in S3 according to lifecycle-expires policy as dictated by Personal Data Protection Act of 3.11 of SRS.

vehicle\_dictionaries is a dictionary table that resides in marketplace-service and consists of the canonical representations of vehicle makes, models, fuels, and transmissions (where models are linked to their parent makes using parent\_id field) and a jsonb field named aliases which gets populated over time with misspelling corrections. This table is used to fill in the pg\_trgm similarity() comparison logic in both search engine and ETL normalization processes which is a must have due to the fact that similarity() function does not support hard-coded arrays which would lose the index. The ingestion-service takes in this dictionary, caches it in memory during initialization and uses the same mechanism that Groq uses for their make/model resolution and thus alias promotion is a mere table update.

Use of S3 keys when passing information between Step Functions states and not the row data itself is an immediate result of the 256 KB state payload limit that a single 100-row chunk of embedding vectors exceeds by about 1.8×
